row.basis: naʿbudu: service after liberation
row.note: The commentary reads naʿbudu as belonging and obedient service rather than a confined rite. After release from Egypt, this verse promises that the people will serve God on the mountain; Hebrew עבד is cognate with the Arabic root in naʿbudu, and the scene redirects an ex-slave community to God.

row.basis: naʿbudu: God owns the liberated servant
row.note: The commentary contrasts belonging to God with Pharaoh's claim over Israel. This verse calls the Israelites God's servants precisely because he brought them out of Egypt, making divine ownership the reason no human master may finally possess them.

row.basis: exclusive fear, service, and oath
row.note: The commentary's first iyyāka binds worship to one addressee. Moses likewise binds Israel's fear, service, and sworn speech to YHWH in a single covenantal command.

row.basis: no other gods after YHWH
row.note: The commentary says the fronted object closes every other possible object of worship. This verse states the corresponding prohibition: Israel must not follow other gods.

row.basis: walk after, obey, serve, cling
row.note: The commentary joins the root-image of a path to worship understood as obedience. This verse gathers walking after God, fearing him, keeping his commands, obeying his voice, serving him, and clinging to him into one sustained allegiance.

row.basis: we will serve YHWH
row.note: The commentary makes the plural naʿbudu a communal declaration that divides one allegiance from rival masters. Joshua's household answer is the same kind of public collective choice: “we will serve YHWH.”

row.basis: remove foreign gods; serve him alone
row.note: The commentary treats exclusive worship as a break with competing objects of service. Samuel makes that sequence explicit: return wholeheartedly, remove foreign gods, direct the heart to YHWH, and serve him alone.

row.basis: refusal of coerced image-worship
row.note: The commentary sets belonging to God against a ruler's power to demand service. The three Judeans tell the king that they will neither serve his gods nor worship his image, even under a death threat.

row.basis: you alone; heaven worships you
row.note: The commentary emphasizes the abrupt collective turn from speaking about God to directly saying “you alone.” Nehemiah's communal prayer begins by directly naming YHWH alone as creator and says that the host of heaven worships him.

row.basis: come, bow, kneel before our maker
row.note: The commentary explains naʿbudu as embodied humility and full submission. This communal summons joins bowing and kneeling to worship before the God who made the worshippers.

row.basis: not to us, but to your name
row.note: The commentary makes the addressee precede the speaker's own act: “you” comes before “we worship.” This plural prayer similarly removes glory from “us” and places God's name first.

row.basis: servants' eyes on a master's hand
row.note: The commentary's owned-servant image does not reduce worship to servility; the servant looks to the one able to give help. The psalm compares the community's eyes toward YHWH with servants watching a master's hand until he shows mercy.

row.basis: your servant; bonds loosed
row.note: The commentary connects being God's servant with release from other masters. The psalmist directly says “I am your servant” and credits YHWH with loosening his bonds.

row.basis: I am yours; save me
row.note: The commentary reads “we worship you and ask you for help” as a voiced acknowledgment of belonging. This verse places possession and petition together in the first person: “I am yours; save me.”

row.basis: our help in the creator's name
row.note: The commentary's second iyyāka directs communal help-seeking to God alone. This concluding plural confession locates “our help” in the name of YHWH, maker of heaven and earth.

row.basis: our soul waits; he is our help
row.note: The commentary insists that worship and asking for aid remain distinct acts addressed to the same one. The psalm's corporate voice waits for YHWH and names him both “our help” and shield.

row.basis: help from maker of heaven and earth
row.note: The commentary says the requested avn is not merely an instrument but is sought from God. This pilgrim confession identifies the source of help as YHWH, maker of heaven and earth.

row.basis: cry in distress; God hears
row.note: The commentary connects direct address with the God who answers those who call. In a named crisis, the psalmist calls to YHWH and cries to his God; the verse answers the plea with God's hearing from his temple.

row.basis: help us because we rely on you
row.note: The commentary distinguishes a concrete need from the one ultimately asked for help. Asa's public prayer names YHWH as uniquely able to help the weak against the strong and asks “help us” because the people rely on him.

row.basis: stand before you and cry for salvation
row.note: The commentary places help-seeking within worship rather than outside it. Jehoshaphat's community says that in disaster it will stand before God at his house, cry to him in distress, and expect him to hear and save.

row.basis: we have no power; our eyes are on you
row.note: The commentary's plural speaker admits dependence without specifying every possible distress. Facing a particular army, this communal prayer confesses that it has no power and turns its eyes only toward God.

row.basis: seeking Egypt for help instead of YHWH
row.note: The commentary contrasts tools and human allies with the one from whom help is to be sought. Isaiah rebukes those who look to Egypt's horses and chariots for aid while not looking to or seeking YHWH.

row.basis: I hold your hand; I will help you
row.note: The commentary's exhausted-traveler image joins a request for help to support that makes walking possible. Here God takes Israel by the hand and explicitly says, “I will help you.”

row.basis: creator who spread out earth alone
row.note: The commentary says God receives worship and help-seeking but needs no helper himself. This creator declaration stresses that YHWH stretched out the heavens alone and spread out the earth by himself.

row.basis: cry to chosen gods; let them save
row.note: The commentary exposes the contradiction of asking powerless objects for aid. Israel is told to cry to the gods it chose and let them save it in trouble, a deliberately negative counterpart to asking God for help.

row.basis: an idol cannot answer or save
row.note: The commentary says a worshipped other cannot remove distress or supply help. Isaiah's carried image remains fixed; when one cries to it, it cannot answer or save from trouble.

row.basis: pitched vessel made watertight
row.note: The commentary develops the root's secondary image of a ship sealed with pitch so that it can endure water. This verse commands Noah to coat the ark inside and out with pitch, the same concrete act of making a wooden vessel water-resistant.

row.basis: bitumen and pitch on a basket-ark
row.note: The commentary's tarred-ship image is about a vulnerable vessel made able to withstand the water. Moses' mother coats the basket-ark with bitumen and pitch before setting it on the Nile.

row.basis: worship after being led on the way
row.note: The commentary lets the support-seeking traveler and the coming request for the road resonate within 1:5. Abraham's servant bows in worship because YHWH led him on the right way to his destination.

row.basis: show me the way I should walk
row.note: The commentary says help asked in 1:5 immediately opens toward the next request for guidance. This direct prayer lifts the self to God and asks to be shown the way in which to walk.

row.basis: bless at all times; ask for straight paths
row.note: The commentary treats worship and help as continuing present acts and connects aid to the road. Tobit's instruction tells a traveler to bless God at all times and ask him to make one's ways straight and one's paths successful.

row.basis: no caller on the Lord is overlooked
row.note: The commentary's direct address presupposes that God hears a caller seeking help. Ben Sira asks readers to recall whether anyone who called on the Lord was ever overlooked, making remembered answered prayer the ground of trust.

row.basis: helper of oppressed and weak
row.note: The commentary describes avn as support for one who cannot bear the burden alone. Judith's prayer calls God helper of the oppressed, supporter of the weak, protector of the forsaken, and savior of the hopeless.

row.basis: victory's strength comes from heaven
row.note: The commentary distinguishes human capacity from the divine help asked for in a threatened task. Judas tells his outnumbered force that victory is not determined by army size because strength comes from heaven.

row.basis: obedience rather than mere sacrifice
row.note: The commentary expands naʿbudu beyond timed ritual into obedient belonging. Samuel contrasts sacrifice with obeying YHWH's voice, so the text tests worship by submission in action.

row.basis: worship and serve God alone
row.note: The commentary reads the fronted iyyāka as an exclusion of every rival object of worship. Jesus answers the tempter with the same double claim: worship the Lord God and serve him alone.

row.basis: God to whom I belong and whom I serve
row.note: The commentary makes naʿbudu a declaration of both ownership and worship. In a crisis at sea, Paul describes God with the paired relation “whose I am” and “whom I serve.”

row.basis: freed from sin, enslaved to God
row.note: The commentary opposes belonging to God to service under other enslaving powers. Paul describes release from sin as becoming enslaved to God, with sanctification and life as the result.

row.basis: bought at a price; not human slaves
row.note: The commentary sets divine ownership against becoming another person's possessed servant. Paul tells the community that it was bought at a price and therefore must not become slaves of human beings.

row.basis: obey God rather than human beings
row.note: The commentary glosses worship as obedient submission and contrasts it with a human authority's demand. Peter and the apostles answer a governing prohibition by saying that obedience belongs to God rather than humans.

row.basis: turn from idols to serve the living God
row.note: The commentary makes exclusive worship both a turning from other objects and a turn toward God. Paul recounts the Thessalonians' conversion from idols to serve a living and true God.

row.basis: sacrifice to demons, not God
row.note: The commentary treats worship wrongly directed to another as allegiance with real consequences. Paul warns that pagan sacrifice makes participants sharers with demons rather than with God.

row.basis: whole embodied life as worship
row.note: The commentary rejects a reduction of worship to bounded ritual times. Paul calls for the presenting of whole bodies as a living sacrifice and names that all-of-life offering as worship.

row.basis: serve the Lord Christ in ordinary work
row.note: The commentary says one master changes the meaning of every act, not just formal devotion. In instructions to workers, Paul identifies the ultimate recipient of service as the Lord Christ rather than the human workplace.

row.basis: serve by strength God supplies
row.note: The commentary holds worship and the help needed to carry it out together without confusing them. This verse directs the one who serves to do so from the strength that God supplies, so that God is glorified.

row.basis: God equips people to do his will
row.note: The commentary presents help-seeking as internal to sustained obedience. This benediction asks God to equip the hearers with every good thing for doing his will and to work in them what pleases him.

row.basis: the Lord is my helper
row.note: The commentary's nesteʿīnu names God as the one asked for help. The Christian speaker can therefore confess, in the words of the verse, that the Lord is “my helper” and need not fear people.

row.basis: approach God for timely help
row.note: The commentary depicts direct address as a request made within worship. This verse invites believers to draw near confidently to God's throne in order to receive mercy and find grace for help at the needed time.

row.basis: one voice directly addresses the creator
row.note: The commentary gives theological weight to a plural community speaking directly to God. The gathered church raises one voice and addresses the Sovereign Lord as maker of heaven, earth, sea, and all within them.

row.basis: collective prayer for strength to speak
row.note: The commentary's “we ask you for help” joins a common task to a direct petition. Under threat, the church asks the Lord to notice the threats and grant his servants boldness for their speech.

row.basis: our Father: plural direct address
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that even a lone reciter says “we” while addressing God as “you.” Jesus' model prayer begins with the communal direct address “Our Father,” before its petitions.

row.basis: give us our daily bread
row.note: The commentary separates worship from help-seeking while binding each to the same addressee. This petition keeps the plural voice and directly asks God for the day's needed provision.

row.basis: angel refuses worship; worship God
row.note: The commentary's angel scene rejects the transfer of worship from God to a creature. The angel in this scene refuses John’s prostration, calls himself a fellow servant, and directs him to worship God.

row.basis: submit to God; resist the devil
row.note: The commentary links exclusive divine allegiance with protection from Satan's authority. James places those acts together: submit to God, resist the devil, and the devil will flee.

row.basis: the evil one does not touch God's-born
row.note: The commentary says belonging to God limits Satan's power over the devoted. This verse states that the evil one does not touch the one born from God, grounding protection in divine keeping.

row.basis: the Lord strengthens and guards from evil
row.note: The commentary combines reliance on the Lord with freedom from the adversary's authority. Paul calls the Lord faithful and says he will strengthen the community and guard it from the evil one.

row.basis: God is not served as one needing help
row.note: The commentary sharply distinguishes the worshipper who needs aid from God, who needs no helper. Paul's Areopagus speech says God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, because he gives life, breath, and all things.

row.basis: direct divine confession to the risen Jesus
row.note: The commentary reserves the first direct “you” and exclusive worship-address for God. In this Christian resurrection scene Thomas addresses Jesus himself as “my Lord and my God,” making the different object of direct confession a material comparison.

row.basis: direct petition to Lord Jesus
row.note: The commentary treats asking help as speech directed only to God. While dying, Stephen invokes the Lord Jesus and asks him to receive his spirit; the Christian scene therefore relocates a direct final petition to Jesus.

row.basis: angels called to worship the Son
row.note: The commentary's heavenly scene has angels refuse worship and turn it back to God. This verse, in its Christian enthronement argument, commands God's angels to worship the Son, so the angelic relation becomes a pointed contrary reading.

row.basis: highway where the traveler does not stray
row.note: The commentary treats the trodden-path image in naʿbudu as preparation for the surah's next request for a straight way. Isaiah's holy highway is a specific travel image in which even the wayfarer does not go astray.

row.basis: a journey too great for the exhausted traveler
row.note: The commentary develops the root's stranded traveler as one who needs support before the next request for guidance. An angel tells exhausted Elijah to rise and eat because the journey is too great for him, making provision the condition of continuing the way.

row.basis: walk without fainting through hope in YHWH
row.note: The commentary's image of help under a burden includes endurance rather than escape from every task. Isaiah says those who wait for YHWH receive renewed strength and can walk without fainting.

row.basis: Aaron and Hur hold up Moses' heavy hands
row.note: The commentary distinguishes human assistance from the divine source to whom help is asked. This battle scene gives the physical image of two companions supporting Moses' failing hands, a concrete human form of shared avn-like help.

row.basis: Jonathan strengthens David's hand in God
row.note: The commentary allows people to assist one another while locating ultimate reliance in God. Jonathan's help is specifically to strengthen David's hand “in God,” rather than to replace God as the ground of security.

row.basis: one lifts a companion who falls
row.note: The commentary explicitly says help can occur among people as well as being asked of God. Qoheleth gives the simple travel-like image of one companion raising the other when one falls.

row.basis: foreigners join themselves to serve YHWH
row.note: The commentary says the “we” of worship is not closed to those arriving from elsewhere. Isaiah names foreigners who join themselves to YHWH in order to serve him and love his name.

row.basis: house of prayer for all peoples
row.note: The commentary's plural worshipper belongs to a community whose address can gather others. This verse calls God's house a house of prayer for all peoples, extending communal direct prayer beyond one ethnic group.

row.basis: servants of YHWH protected from attack
row.note: The commentary says belonging to the sole master protects against a hostile power. Isaiah calls the defeat of weapons and accusations the heritage of YHWH's servants, a parallel protection image without making the adversary Satan in this verse.

row.basis: the adversary's permission is bounded
row.note: The commentary says Satan has no unconstrained authority over God's servants. Job's trial gives a qualified analogue: God permits the adversary access to Job's goods but explicitly sets a limit, so it clarifies protection as bounded testing rather than effortless immunity.

row.basis: travelers' prayer for straight steps and deliverance
row.note: The commentary's support-seeking traveler makes the road a place of dependence. The Babylonian Talmud's travelers' prayer asks God to lead and direct one's steps in peace and to deliver the traveler from danger.

row.basis: God works willing and acting within believers
row.note: The commentary says the servant's ongoing acts need divine help without ceasing to be the servant's acts. Paul says God is at work in believers both to will and to work for his good pleasure.

row.basis: community helps through intercessory prayer
row.note: The commentary separates the human help that can be offered from the God to whom aid is ultimately directed. Paul says the Corinthians help him through prayer, so their shared action participates in God's deliverance rather than displacing it.

row.basis: bear one another's burdens
row.note: The commentary calls avn support that stands behind another's burden and also permits mutual help. This instruction makes that image ethical: the community is to carry one another's burdens.

row.basis: pray without ceasing
row.note: The commentary hears the imperfect verbs “we worship” and “we ask help” as ongoing rather than completed acts. Paul's compact command to pray without ceasing supplies a Christian formulation of that continuing posture.

row.basis: Lord's Prayer recited three times daily
row.note: The commentary reflects on a communal direct address repeated within regular worship without becoming merely a one-time formula. The Didache directs believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day, an early Christian practice that makes a plural address and petitions habitual.

row.basis: angels as ministering servants sent to aid heirs
row.note: The commentary distinguishes angels from the one to be worshipped and allows creaturely assistance under God. This verse defines angels as ministering spirits sent for the benefit of those inheriting salvation, supplying a Christian hierarchy of worship above angelic service.

row.basis: bowing to images and serving them
row.note: The commentary's object-first iyyāka excludes every alternate object of worship. This command joins the two forbidden acts in one verse: bowing to carved images and serving them.

row.basis: YHWH or Baal; stop wavering
row.note: The commentary treats exclusive worship as a decisive separation from competing masters. Elijah forces the same choice before Israel: if YHWH is God, follow him; if Baal, follow him.

row.basis: fearing YHWH while serving other gods
row.note: The commentary insists that a single confession cannot leave competing objects in place. This verse names the divided arrangement directly: the people fear YHWH while continuing to serve their own gods.

row.basis: God's glory given to no other
row.note: The commentary understands “you alone” as a refusal to transfer divine honor elsewhere. YHWH's self-declaration likewise withholds his glory from another and his praise from images.

row.basis: no savior besides YHWH
row.note: The commentary says that help finally comes from the one addressed in worship. This verse makes the exclusion explicit in saving language: apart from YHWH there is no savior.

row.basis: turn to me and be saved; no other God
row.note: The commentary's direct address makes the worshipper turn to the sole source of aid. Isaiah summons the ends of the earth to turn to God and be saved because he is God and there is no other.

row.basis: created by God and called his
row.note: The commentary grounds belonging to God in creation before it becomes a spoken act of worship. This direct divine address joins creation, redemption, naming, and possession: “you are mine.”

row.basis: all gifts come from God first
row.note: The commentary says the worshipper seeks help from God while God needs no supporting power. David's corporate prayer admits that people can offer only what already comes from God: “from your own hand we have given you.”

row.basis: God does not need creatures' offerings
row.note: The commentary denies that God has the weakness or need for a helper. In a sacrifice-focused speech, God says that even if he were hungry he would not tell the worshipper, because the world and all within it are his.

row.basis: God's own arm brings salvation
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the worshipper who asks help from the God who does not require it. This verse says that when God found no helper, his own arm brought salvation and his own wrath sustained him.

row.basis: arm of flesh versus God who helps
row.note: The commentary allows human means but refuses to make them the final ground of aid. Hezekiah contrasts the enemy's “arm of flesh” with YHWH, who is with Judah to help it and fight its battles.

row.basis: God supports the hand of one who falls
row.note: The commentary's traveler image includes help that keeps a person from collapsing under the way's burden. This verse says that though the faithful person falls, YHWH upholds that person's hand.

row.basis: God's hand leads and holds the traveler
row.note: The commentary connects help with guidance on the way. The psalmist says that even at the farthest place God's hand will lead and his right hand will hold him fast.

row.basis: God guides the redeemed people to his dwelling
row.note: The commentary makes the plural worshipper a community whose help opens toward a journey and destination. The song after the sea says that God's steadfast love led the people he redeemed and guided them toward his holy habitation.

row.basis: teach your way; unite my heart to fear your name
row.note: The commentary joins a single object of worship to the road imagery and to a heart not divided among masters. This prayer asks God to teach his way and to make the speaker's heart one in fearing God's name.

row.basis: worship God in spirit and truth
row.note: The commentary extends worship beyond a narrow set of ritual acts into a whole posture of submission. Jesus' saying defines fitting worship by its relation to God's Spirit and truth rather than to an external location or rite.

row.basis: bowing before Jesus and saying “Lord, help me”
row.note: The commentary directs both worship and the explicit request for help to Allah alone. In this healing scene, the woman bows before Jesus and addresses to him the direct plea, “Lord, help me,” forming a particularly close Christian counter-narrative.

row.basis: one God, the Father; one Lord, Jesus Christ
row.note: The commentary's exclusive divine address has one undivided addressee. Paul preserves “one God, the Father” while placing “one Lord, Jesus Christ” within the same creational confession, a distinctively Christian reconfiguration of exclusive devotion.

row.basis: every knee bends at Jesus' name
row.note: The commentary treats bodily submission in worship as due only to God. This eschatological Christian scene says that every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth will bend at Jesus' name.

row.basis: every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord
row.note: The commentary's direct confession separates the one worshipped from all rivals. This verse gives universal confession of Jesus Christ as Lord while directing the resulting glory to God the Father, a two-term Christian formulation absent from the commentary's formula.

row.basis: shared heavenly praise of God and the Lamb
row.note: The commentary's heavenly worship returns praise away from creatures to God alone. Revelation's universal hymn offers blessing, honor, glory, and might together to the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb, an explicit alternative heavenly distribution of praise.

row.basis: asking the Father in Jesus' name
row.note: The commentary makes direct petition itself part of exclusive worship. Jesus instructs disciples to ask the Father in his name, providing a Christian pattern of petition mediated through Jesus.

row.basis: one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus
row.note: The commentary's worshipper addresses God without a named mediating figure. This confession likewise says “one God” but adds one mediator between God and humanity, the human Christ Jesus.

row.basis: the Spirit helps weakness in prayer
row.note: The commentary makes asking for help an act inside worship and acknowledges that the burden exceeds the worshipper's strength. Paul says the Spirit helps human weakness precisely where people do not know how to pray as they ought.

row.basis: Jesus asks the Father to keep disciples from the evil one
row.note: The commentary links belonging and reliance on God to protection from Satan's authority. Jesus' prayer asks the Father not to remove the disciples from the world but to keep them from the evil one.

row.basis: grace sufficient in weakness
row.note: The commentary presents help as what enables a servant to stand under a task rather than as an escape from all burden. The divine reply to Paul calls grace sufficient and power perfected in weakness.

row.basis: make every request known to God
row.note: The commentary leaves the object of aid in 1:5 deliberately open to every need while fixing its addressee. Paul likewise tells believers to bring requests about everything to God by prayer, petition, and thanksgiving.

row.basis: God restores, confirms, strengthens, establishes
row.note: The commentary's help supports endurance beneath worship's weight and protects the devoted. This promise says that after suffering, the God of all grace will restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish the believers.

row.basis: in life and death, we belong to the Lord
row.note: The commentary stretches worship beyond a momentary rite into a declaration of who owns one's whole life. Paul says that whether believers live or die, they are the Lord's.

row.basis: bought at a price; glorify God in the body
row.note: The commentary makes belonging to God encompass more than a discrete ritual act. This verse joins being bought at a price to the command to glorify God in the body.

row.basis: offer acceptable worship with reverence and awe
row.note: The commentary glosses worship as humility carried to its limit. Hebrews calls the community to offer acceptable worship with reverence and awe in response to the kingdom it receives.

row.basis: servants worship day and night and are sheltered
row.note: The commentary's “we” is a protected community whose worship is ongoing. Revelation pictures the multitude before God's throne serving him day and night, while the enthroned one shelters them.

row.basis: the church prays earnestly to God for Peter
row.note: The commentary uses a plural voice for direct aid-seeking within a community. During Peter's imprisonment, the church's response is persistent prayer to God on his behalf.

row.basis: the Lord stands by and strengthens the servant
row.note: The commentary's avn is support that stands behind a burdened person. Paul reports that the Lord stood by him and strengthened him for the proclamation entrusted to him.

row.basis: acknowledge God in all ways; paths made straight
row.note: The commentary lets 1:5's help-seeking reach forward to the straight path while keeping God before the worshipper's own action. Proverbs says that acknowledging God in all one's ways results in God making one's paths straight.

row.basis: send wisdom to labor alongside the petitioner
row.note: The commentary says aid can be an enabling companion while its ultimate source remains God. Solomon's prayer asks God to send Wisdom from the holy heavens so that she may be with him and labor with him.

row.basis: make God's will one's own will
row.note: The commentary explains worship as obedient belonging, not a merely timed ceremony. This rabbinic maxim tells the disciple to make God's will like one's own will and to set aside one's own will before God's.
